correctness.rationale: Exact CRT equivalence reconstructs the infinite problem as one residue class per distinct prime. For the odd five-prime case all remaining primes exceed seven and therefore cover at most one position in any block of length at most 11. The eight-row certificate enumerates every one of at most 105 small-prime residue tuples, establishing both attainable length j-1 and impossibility of lengths j and 11. For even support, J(2a)=2J(a) is proved using odd-progressions modulo odd a, and the odd-four-prime classification is established by explicit cover and capacity bounds, including the necessary overlap at length seven. All exponents and boundary cases are included. The actual embedded Python program independently verifies all certificate values and eight entire radical periods; finite sample checks are not substituted for proof.

originality.rationale: The all-integers omega=5 eight-fiber divisibility classification is strictly stronger than the previously known maximum H(5)=14: all seven nonmaximum values and rigidity under replacement of arbitrary large primes are determined. Hajdu–Saradha (2012) proves maxima and mandatory primes but does not state the intermediate fibers in its inspected full text. OEIS tables and general bounds do not entail the exact support threshold without this finite exhaustive proof. Earlier unindexed or implicit coverage remains a residual risk.

value.rationale: Jacobsthal’s function controls gaps between reduced residues, a classical sieve invariant used in prime-gap and coprimality questions. The exact eight-level partition for every integer with five distinct prime factors resolves a natural fixed-support classification, not a selectively chosen finite interval. It identifies complete rigidity under changes in arbitrarily large prime factors and determines all nonmaximal values below the known extremum H(5)=14, giving a reusable small-prime cutoff in residue-cover analysis. Neither the historical maximum nor generic large-k bounds imply this partition; the limitation to exactly five prime factors is explicit.
